sections.guidingQuestion: What must happen before two daughter cells inherit complete copies of a chromosome?
sections.explanation:
DNA replication produces copies with the same base sequence as the original DNA. It is required for reproduction and for growth and tissue replacement in multicellular organisms, so new cells inherit genetic instructions. Copying is highly accurate, though rare errors can persist as mutations.

Replication copies DNA into DNA; transcription uses a selected DNA region to make RNA. Replication preserves genetic information for new cells, whereas transcription allows that information to be expressed.
sections.revisionSummary: It produces DNA copies with identical base sequences for reproduction, growth and tissue replacement, allowing new cells to inherit genetic instructions.
terms: DNA replication: synthesis of new DNA with the same base sequence as the template
Chromosome: DNA molecule with associated proteins that carries genetic information
sections.workedExample: A skin basal cell duplicates its genomic DNA before mitosis so its daughters can continue producing skin tissue.

sections.guidingQuestion: After semi-conservative replication, each daughter DNA duplex contains which strands?
sections.explanation:
The two parental DNA strands separate. Each is a template for a complementary new strand. Each daughter double helix therefore contains one original strand and one new strand: replication is semi-conservative.

A pairs with T and G with C, so the template sequence determines the order of nucleotides in the new strand. A template segment TACG produces the complementary segment ATGC. Complementarity allows a high degree of accuracy; it does not mean errors are impossible.
sections.revisionSummary: Each original strand templates a new strand using A–T and G–C pairing. Each daughter double helix has one original and one new strand, allowing accurate sequence copying.
terms: Semi-conservative replication: each daughter DNA double helix contains one parental strand and one newly made strand
Complementary base pairing: A pairs with T and G with C in DNA
sections.workedExample: A DNA strand with bases TACG templates a complementary strand ATGC. Each new double helix contains one original strand.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the immediate action of helicase at a replication fork?
sections.explanation:
Helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two DNA strands. The covalent sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact.

DNA polymerase uses each exposed strand as a template, selecting complementary DNA nucleotides and joining them by covalent phosphodiester bonds to form a new strand. Helicase separates existing strands; DNA polymerase synthesizes their complementary copies.
sections.revisionSummary: Helicase unwinds DNA and breaks interstrand hydrogen bonds. DNA polymerase joins complementary DNA nucleotides along the exposed templates.
terms: Helicase: enzyme that unwinds DNA and separates paired strands by disrupting hydrogen bonds
DNA polymerase: enzyme that adds DNA nucleotides to a growing complementary strand

sections.guidingQuestion: Which sequence of conditions describes one ordinary PCR cycle?
sections.explanation:
A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers. The chosen primers define the target; repeated cycles can produce many copies of the region. PCR is not the same as replication of an entire chromosome.

DNA has a negatively charged sugar–phosphate backbone, so an electric field draws fragments toward the positive electrode. In an appropriate gel, shorter DNA fragments generally travel farther than longer ones. Compare bands against a DNA ladder to estimate length; a matching band position does not reveal the fragment's complete base sequence.
sections.revisionSummary: PCR uses repeated temperature cycles, primers and thermostable Taq polymerase to amplify selected DNA. Electrophoresis separates negatively charged fragments toward the positive electrode; shorter fragments usually travel farther.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why are several independent DNA markers used in forensic profiling?
sections.explanation:
PCR amplifies selected DNA regions from small samples. Electrophoresis separates the amplified fragments by length, allowing informative markers to be compared in forensic investigations and paternity testing. In parentage analysis, each child’s alleles must be compatible with contributions from the biological parents.

A match at one marker does not establish identity: different people can share that fragment length. Using more independent markers reduces the probability of a false match. This illustrates how additional measurements increase reliability. Contamination, mixtures, close relatives and sample handling still affect interpretation; classroom profiles are illustrative rather than evidence from a real case.
sections.revisionSummary: PCR and electrophoresis allow comparison of markers for forensics and paternity. Multiple independent markers reduce coincidental false matches; one matching band is insufficient.
terms: DNA profile: pattern of DNA markers used to compare biological samples
Genetic marker: detectable DNA region that differs among individuals
False match: apparent agreement between samples that do not have the same source
sections.workedExample: A disputed parentage case compares several inherited short tandem repeat markers, rather than relying on a single PCR band.

misconceptions.misconception: One matching DNA band establishes the donor's identity with certainty.
misconceptions.correction: A reliable identification integrates multiple markers, controls and statistical interpretation.

sections.guidingQuestion: At which end can DNA polymerase add the next nucleotide?
sections.explanation:
Why DNA strands have direction. Each nucleotide's sugar has numbered carbons. A DNA strand has a 5′ end and a 3′ end; the 3′ end exposes a hydroxyl group to which DNA polymerase can add the next deoxyribonucleotide. The incoming nucleotide is joined through its 5′ phosphate, forming a phosphodiester bond in the sugar–phosphate backbone. Consequently, a daughter strand can elongate only in the 5′→3′ direction, even though the parent strand being copied is read 3′→5′.

Apply the rule to a real sequence. For a template written 3′–TACG–5′, complementary pairing yields a newly synthesized strand 5′–ATGC–3′. If instead the template is displayed 5′→3′, first reverse its orientation before writing the daughter sequence 5′→3′. Do not confuse a strand's written direction with the replication fork's direction of movement. Both new daughter strands grow 5′→3′; because the two parental strands are antiparallel, one new strand can follow fork opening continuously and the other must be assembled in segments.

Why a primer is necessary. DNA polymerase extends an existing 3′ end; it does not normally start a DNA chain from isolated free nucleotides. Primase supplies a short RNA primer, and subsequent enzymes replace primer material and seal discontinuities. The separate leading- and lagging-strand machinery is explained in D1.1.7–D1.1.8 (HL).
sections.revisionSummary: It adds the incoming nucleotide’s 5′ phosphate to the growing strand’s free 3′ hydroxyl, extending DNA 5′→3′ while reading the template 3′→5′.
terms: 5′ end: end of a DNA strand with a phosphate associated with sugar carbon 5′
3′ end: end with the sugar's free 3′ hydroxyl group (–OH)
Antiparallel: the two DNA strands run in opposite 5′→3′ directions
sections.workedExample: For template 3′-ACGT-5′ read from left to right, polymerase extends 5′-TGCA-3′ toward the right.

misconceptions.misconception: DNA polymerase sometimes builds new DNA 3′→5′ on the lagging strand.
misconceptions.correction: Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′.

sections.guidingQuestion: What distinguishes the newly synthesized lagging strand from the leading strand?
sections.explanation:
On the leading-strand template, a newly primed strand is extended continuously in the same overall direction in which the replication fork opens. Because the polymerase can only extend a 3′ end, the leading template is read 3′→5′ toward the fork.

The opposite template polarity requires repeated RNA primers on the lagging strand. Each Okazaki fragment still grows 5′→3′, but away from the advancing fork; the RNA primers are later replaced and ligase joins the fragments. The leading strand instead grows continuously toward the fork after its initial primer.
sections.revisionSummary: Both grow 5′→3′. The leading strand is continuous toward the advancing fork after one RNA primer; the lagging strand is discontinuous, with a new RNA primer for each Okazaki fragment growing away from the fork.
terms: Leading strand: daughter strand synthesized continuously toward the advancing replication fork
Lagging strand: daughter strand synthesized discontinuously away from the fork
Okazaki fragment: short DNA segment made from a new primer on the lagging strand
sections.workedExample: At a right-moving fork, an individual Okazaki fragment begins nearer the fork and grows to the left; the leading daughter grows to the right.

misconceptions.correction: Okazaki fragments are individually synthesized 5′→3′, but in the direction opposite fork travel.

sections.guidingQuestion: In bacterial DNA replication, which enzyme mainly extends new DNA from RNA primers?
sections.explanation:
DNA polymerase cannot begin a new DNA strand without an existing free 3′ end. In the IB's prokaryotic model, DNA primase builds a short RNA primer complementary to the template. That primer provides the 3′ end from which DNA polymerase III can begin extending a daughter strand. This is why primase must act before polymerase III on each new segment.

DNA polymerase III adds complementary DNA nucleotides to the primer's 3′ end, synthesizing the daughter strand in the 5′→3′ direction. On the leading strand this extension can continue towards the fork after an initial primer; on the lagging strand a fresh primer is needed for each Okazaki fragment because each fragment grows away from the opening fork.

DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primer and replaces its nucleotides with DNA. This still leaves a nick in the sugar–phosphate backbone between adjacent DNA segments. DNA ligase closes that nick by forming the missing covalent connection. Polymerase I replaces nucleotide material; ligase joins the backbone. These polymerase names refer to the specified prokaryotic model, not to all eukaryotic replication enzymes.
sections.revisionSummary: Primase makes RNA primers; polymerase III extends DNA; polymerase I replaces RNA primers with DNA; ligase seals remaining backbone nicks.
terms: Primase: enzyme making short RNA primers that supply free 3′ ends
DNA polymerase III: main DNA-extending polymerase in the specified bacterial system
DNA polymerase I: bacterial enzyme that removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA
DNA ligase: enzyme sealing nicks between adjacent DNA fragments
sections.workedExample: Imagine three Okazaki fragments: primase must start each one; polymerase III extends each; polymerase I replaces their RNA primers; ligase seals the resulting nicks. All three fragments were built 5′→3′.

misconceptions.misconception: The enzyme that extends DNA also makes RNA primers and seals all remaining nicks.
misconceptions.correction: Primase starts RNA primers; polymerase III extends DNA; polymerase I replaces primer RNA; ligase seals backbone nicks.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which activity directly removes a mismatched terminal nucleotide during bacterial polymerase III proofreading?
sections.explanation:
During prokaryotic replication, DNA polymerase III can detect a mismatched nucleotide at the growing strand’s 3′ end. It removes this terminal nucleotide by its 3′→5′ exonuclease activity; it does not remove the corresponding template base.

A correctly matched nucleotide is then added and normal 5′→3′ synthesis resumes. Proofreading greatly improves accuracy, but some errors escape and can become mutations. Other repair pathways are separate from the polymerase III action required here.
sections.revisionSummary: It removes a mismatched nucleotide from the growing strand’s 3′ end, then replaces it with a correctly matched nucleotide and resumes synthesis.
terms: Proofreading: checking newly added DNA bases and correcting mismatches during replication
3′→5′ exonuclease: enzyme activity that removes nucleotides from a strand's 3′ end
sections.workedExample: If a new G is paired opposite template G by mistake, polymerase III can excise terminal G and insert the complementary C.

questions.prompt: A cell enters mitosis without duplicating its chromosomal DNA, although it has synthesized many proteins. Which process was missing for both daughter cells to receive complete copies of the chromosomes?

options.feedback: DNA replication produces two copies of each chromosome's sequence; subsequent chromosome segregation can then distribute one copy to each daughter cell.

options.text: Translation of every mRNA into protein
options.feedback: Translation uses ribosomes to make proteins from mRNA. Making proteins does not copy the DNA sequences that daughter cells inherit.

options.text: Breaking every phosphodiester bond in each chromosome
options.feedback: Phosphodiester bonds form the sugar–phosphate backbone. Replication separates base-paired strands without destroying the entire DNA backbone.

options.text: Replacing thymine in DNA with uracil
options.feedback: Uracil is ordinarily found in RNA; DNA replication preserves complementary DNA base pairing (A–T, C–G) rather than converting DNA to RNA.

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA replication is required for reproduction, growth and tissue replacement. [3]
questions.answer: Replication copies the DNA base sequence before cells divide. New cells inherit the genetic instructions needed for their functions. Repeated division with copied DNA supplies cells for growth and replacement and passes genetic information during reproduction.
markingPoints: Replication copies the DNA base sequence before cells divide.
New cells inherit the genetic instructions needed for their functions.
Repeated division with copied DNA supplies cells for growth and replacement and passes genetic information during reproduction.

questions.prompt: After semi-conservative replication, each daughter DNA duplex contains which strands?

options.text: One parental and one new strand
options.feedback: Each original strand templates a new complementary strand, so each daughter DNA duplex contains one parental and one newly synthesized strand.
Keeping both parental strands together in one duplex describes the conservative model, not semiconservative replication.
Daughter DNA is related to the parental molecule by complementary base pairing; new strands are not random unrelated molecules.
Each daughter duplex retains one original template strand; a duplex containing only new strands is not the semiconservative outcome.

questions.prompt: Explain how semi-conservative replication and complementary base pairing produce accurate DNA copies. [3]
questions.answer: Each original DNA strand serves as a template for a new strand. A pairs with T and G with C, determining the new strand’s sequence. Each daughter double helix contains one original strand and one complementary new strand.
markingPoints: Each original DNA strand serves as a template for a new strand.
A pairs with T and G with C, determining the new strand’s sequence.
Each daughter double helix contains one original strand and one complementary new strand.

questions.prompt: What is the immediate action of helicase at a replication fork?

options.text: Separate DNA strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds
options.feedback: Helicase unwinds the parental duplex by disrupting hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; covalent sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact.

options.text: Join Okazaki fragments by covalent bonds
options.feedback: DNA ligase seals nicks in the sugar–phosphate backbone between Okazaki fragments; helicase unwinds double-stranded DNA.
Ribosomes join amino acids during protein synthesis; helicase acts on DNA base pairs, not peptide formation.
RNA primer removal and replacement involve nucleases and DNA polymerase, not helicase's strand-separation function.

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of helicase and DNA polymerase in replication, distinguishing the bonds affected. [3]
questions.answer: Helicase unwinds DNA and breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. The parental sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact. DNA polymerase selects complementary nucleotides and joins them by covalent phosphodiester bonds in new strands.
markingPoints: Helicase unwinds DNA and breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
The parental sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact.
DNA polymerase selects complementary nucleotides and joins them by covalent phosphodiester bonds in new strands.

questions.prompt: Which sequence of conditions describes one ordinary PCR cycle?

options.feedback: Correct. A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers.
Consider why “Translation, transcription, replication” does not answer this question. DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode.
Consider why “Polymerase extension, protein folding, mitosis” does not answer this question. DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode.
Consider why “Gel separation, ligation, protein sorting” does not answer this question. DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode.

questions.prompt: Outline how PCR amplifies a selected DNA region. [3]
questions.answer: Heating separates the DNA strands. Cooling allows two primers to bind complementary sequences flanking the target. Thermostable Taq polymerase extends the primers; repeated temperature cycles amplify the target.
markingPoints: Heating separates the DNA strands.
Cooling allows two primers to bind complementary sequences flanking the target.
Thermostable Taq polymerase extends the primers; repeated temperature cycles amplify the target.

questions.prompt: At which end can DNA polymerase add the next nucleotide?

options.text: The free 3′ end of the growing strand
options.feedback: Correct. A DNA strand has chemically different 5′ and 3′ ends because nucleotides have a phosphate-linked 5′ carbon and a hydroxyl-bearing 3′ carbon.

options.text: The 5′ end of the growing strand
options.feedback: Consider why “The 5′ end of the growing strand” does not answer this question. Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′.
Consider why “Either end with equal probability” does not answer this question. Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′.

options.text: The middle of an intact phosphodiester bond
options.feedback: Consider why “The middle of an intact phosphodiester bond” does not answer this question. Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′.

questions.prompt: Explain why both new DNA strands are synthesized 5′→3′. [3]
questions.answer: DNA strands have chemically different 5′ and 3′ ends. DNA polymerase joins an incoming nucleotide’s 5′ phosphate to the free 3′ hydroxyl of the growing strand. Extension is therefore always 5′→3′, while the antiparallel template is read 3′→5′.
markingPoints: DNA strands have chemically different 5′ and 3′ ends.

questions.answer: The templates are antiparallel, but polymerase extends DNA only 5′→3′. The leading strand grows continuously toward the fork after one RNA primer. The lagging strand forms discontinuous Okazaki fragments away from the fork, each needing a new RNA primer.

questions.prompt: An idealized PCR model begins with 20 amplifiable target duplexes and assumes perfect doubling per cycle. Calculate the expected count after four cycles, then explain why a real reaction may produce fewer copies.
questions.answer: 20 × 2⁴ = 320 target duplexes in this idealized model. Actual reaction efficiency can be reduced by reagent limitations, incomplete primer annealing or inhibition; amplification will not always double perfectly.
markingPoints: Correct multiplication 20 × 2⁴ = 320 duplexes.
One valid mechanism that prevents perfect exponential efficiency.
